home.title: Echoes – free network tools for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, Linux and Android
home.description: Echoes puts 20 network tools in one free, open-source app: a Doctor that tells you why a site won't open, ping, traceroute, a speed test, a port scanner, DNS and WHOIS, cURL, a TLS checker, SSH, an uptime monitor and file sharing with any browser. No account, no ads, no tracking.

hero.pill: Now on the App Store for iPhone, iPad and Mac
hero.title: 20 network tools. One free app.
hero.lede: Find out why a site won't open, test your speed, ping, scan ports, look up DNS and send files to any device. Echoes brings the tools you would normally run one by one into one simple app.
hero.imageAlt: Echoes on a Mac: the Doctor says example.com works from here, with every check it ran
hero.phoneAlt: Echoes on an iPhone: the Doctor

doctor.title: Website not opening? Find out why.
doctor.lede: The Doctor checks everything between you and a site, then tells you in one sentence what is wrong, and what to do about it.

points.title: Your own network
points.text: The adapter, the gateway, a VPN or proxy, and a Wi-Fi login page that is in the way.

points.title: DNS that lies
points.text: Your system's DNS answers are compared with encrypted DNS, so forged answers and known filter addresses stand out.

points.title: Filtering or a blocked address
points.text: TLS is tried with and without the site's name, to tell name filtering (SNI) from a blocked IP address.

points.title: Down for everyone, or just for you?
points.text: The site is also checked from several countries, so you know whether the problem is the site or your connection.

points.title: Would a workaround help?
points.text: Retries with the first packet split in pieces say whether the “fragment” setting in apps such as v2rayNG, Hiddify or Xray would get through.

points.title: A report to share
points.text: Every step with its timing, and a report you can copy for whoever runs the network.

doctor.alt: The Doctor finds SNI filtering: the site's address works, but not with its name

features.title: Simple to use, deep when you need it

items.title: Ping, traceroute and MTR
items.text: Live replies, a latency graph and the numbers that matter, for any host.
points: TCP ping to a port, for hosts that don't answer normal ping.
Packet size, TTL and “don't fragment”, to find the largest packet a path takes.
No admin rights needed: where the system doesn't allow normal ping, Echoes switches to UDP by itself.
An alert when a host goes up or down.
items.alt: Ping on a Mac: TCP ping to 1.1.1.1 port 443 with live replies and a latency graph

items.title: How fast is your internet, really?
items.text: Download, upload, ping and jitter, and how much the delay grows while the line is busy.
points: Cloudflare's nearest data centre, public test servers in more than 20 cities, or a server of your own.
A grade for latency under load (bufferbloat).
Up to 16 connections at once, and your last 20 results.
items.alt: The speed test measuring the download speed against a server in Washington

items.title: Know when a site goes down
items.text: Watches your servers and websites, and tells you when one goes down or comes back.
points: Ping, TCP and HTTP checks, each with its own interval.
Alerts in Telegram, from a bot of your own.
Warnings before a certificate or a domain runs out.
Checks that a page does or doesn't contain some text.
items.alt: The uptime monitor: four sites up and one down, with their history

items.title: Send files to any device

points: HTTPS with the device's own certificate, behind an 8-digit PIN. Browsers warn once, because the certificate is the device's own.
Files both ways, with drag and drop, and downloads that resume.
Each shared file has its own link and QR code.
Or catch webhook requests and see each one in full.
items.alt: The web server sharing files and chat, with its link, PIN and QR code

items.title: DNS, the way you need it

WHOIS through RDAP, with the domain's expiry date.

privacy.title: Echoes collects nothing
privacy.lede: No account, no ads, no analytics and no tracking. Nothing is sent to the developer, who can't see what you test, where you connect or what you save.

items.title: It stays on your device
items.text: Settings, history, notes, saved requests and tokens stay in the app's own folder. Secrets are encrypted, and notes are locked with your master password.

items.title: Nothing runs by itself
items.text: The web server, proxy, request catcher and socket listeners start only when you press Start. On its own, Echoes only checks for a new version, and only in the builds from GitHub.

items.title: Data Not Collected
items.text: That is what the App Store's privacy label says. The source code is public, so you can check it.

privacy.title: Privacy policy – Echoes
privacy.description: Echoes collects no data: what stays on your device, which services some tools use, and the permissions the app asks for.
privacy.heading: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: Echoes is a free, open-source network toolkit (ping, traceroute, port scanner, DNS, SSH, speed test, file-sharing web server and more). This page says what it does with your data. The short version: it collects none.
privacy.sourceNote: This is the same policy as PRIVACY.md in the source code.

sections.title: What the developer collects
paragraphs: Nothing. Echoes has no account, no advertising, no analytics, no crash-reporting service and no tracking SDK. Nothing is sent to the developer, who can't see what you test, where you connect or what you save.

sections.title: What stays on your device
paragraphs: Your settings, the hosts and URLs you typed (history), notes, saved requests, SSH profiles and the tokens you add (Telegram, Cloudflare) are stored only on your device, in the app's own data folder.
list: Secrets (passwords, tokens) are encrypted on disk. Notes and the Cloudflare vault are encrypted with a key made from your master password.
You can export everything to one password-protected backup file and restore it on another device. The file goes only where you save it.
On an iPhone or iPad, the files that browsers send to the file-sharing page are kept in the Echoes folder of the Files app (On My iPhone), so you can open, move or delete them there.
Deleting the app, or its data folder, deletes the data.

sections.title: What leaves your device, and why
paragraphs: Echoes is a network tool, so it makes network requests: the ones you start, to the hosts you ask about, plus a few public services some tools are built on. Those services receive the request itself and so, as with any website you visit, your public IP address. Echoes doesn't control them; each has its own privacy policy.
list: The hosts, ports and URLs you test (ping, traceroute, port scan, cURL, DNS, TLS, SSH, sockets, Doctor).
check-host.net, to test a host from servers around the world.
Speed test servers: speed.cloudflare.com, or the file host you choose (Cloudflare, Tele2, Leaseweb, Linode, Selectel, DataPacket and similar).
Public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers (Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, OpenDNS, AdGuard) when you use the DNS tool.
IP-information providers (ipinfo.io, ipwho.is, ipapi.co, ip-api.com, geojs.io, freeipapi.com, iplocation.net) to look up the IP address you enter, or your own.
RDAP (rdap.org, rdap.verisign.com) for a domain's registration and expiry.
DNS blocklists (Spamhaus, SpamCop, Barracuda) and the domain's own mail records, when you run the mail check on a domain.

Connectivity and public-IP services: well-known sites such as Google, Microsoft and Cloudflare, and connectivitycheck.gstatic.com (the Doctor checks that the internet works), and Cloudflare, ipify, ident.me and icanhazip (Dynamic DNS reads your public IP).

Telegram (api.telegram.org), only if you add your own bot token for uptime alerts, and Cloudflare (api.cloudflare.com), only if you add your own API token. A token stays on your device and is sent only to its own service.
GitHub (api.github.com), only in the builds you download from GitHub, to see whether a newer version exists. Builds from an app store don't check: the store updates the app.

sections.title: Servers Echoes can run
paragraphs: The web server (file sharing and chat), the request catcher, the proxy and the socket listeners start only when you press Start, and stop when you press Stop or quit Echoes. While one runs, a device that can reach its port can connect to it; the file-sharing page asks for a PIN, and data passes only between your device and the devices that connect. Echoes doesn't send it anywhere else.

sections.title: Permissions
list: Network (all platforms): Echoes is a network tool.
Local network (macOS and iOS): asked the first time you scan, ping or share with a device on your local network. If you decline, local devices look unreachable.

Notifications, foreground service and start at boot (Android): for uptime alerts and to keep a scan, monitor or file share running while the app is in the background. Start at boot is off unless you turn it on.
Location (Windows): Windows lets an app see the names of nearby Wi-Fi networks only when location access is on. Echoes reads them locally for the Wi-Fi analyzer and sends them nowhere.

sections.title: Children
paragraphs: Echoes is a general-purpose tool and isn't directed at children. It collects no personal information from anyone.

sections.title: Open source
paragraphs: Echoes is released under the MIT license. Anyone can read the source code, check the claims on this page and build the app: github.com/SinaXhpm/Echoes.

sections.title: Changes
paragraphs: If this policy changes, the new version replaces this page, with a new date at the top.

sections.title: Contact
paragraphs: Questions or concerns: open an issue at github.com/SinaXhpm/Echoes/issues.
